title: A Child of My Own Turns a True-Crime Headline Into an Argument About How Stories Judge Women
dek: Maite Alberdi’s A Child of My Own reaches Netflix after its festival run. Its mixture of reenactment and documentary evidence asks viewers to understand a desperate act without confusing understanding with acquittal.
content:
## The Netflix release changes the size of the jury

Maite Alberdi’s *A Child of My Own* arrives on Netflix on August 13 after screening at festivals including Berlin. The film returns to the case of Eleonor Alejandra Marín Mendoza, a Mexican woman who faked a pregnancy and abducted a newborn. Alberdi does not present that history as a conventional sequence of investigation, arrest and verdict. She combines dramatized scenes, interviews, home video, surveillance material and evidence of the filmmaking process itself.

That form is not an ornamental choice. The case entered public memory as a sensational crime story with a clean headline and an obvious perpetrator. A global streaming release places the story before a much larger jury, one trained by true-crime formats to expect disclosure, suspense and moral resolution. Alberdi interrupts those expectations by showing that every account—including a reenactment designed to generate empathy—is constructed.

The film’s central difficulty is easy to state and hard to solve. It wants to investigate the social and familial pressure placed on a woman who believed she had to become a mother, while keeping the harm done to another woman and child in view. Explanation can resemble excuse when a camera spends more time with the person who caused the harm. Condemnation can become another form of evasion when it treats the crime as inexplicable.

## Pink is part of the evidence

Critics have noted the film’s highly controlled visual design, especially its use of pink around the dramatized version of Alejandra’s life. The color evokes the commercial shorthand of idealized femininity: nursery decorations, gifts, clothing and the public performance of an expected pregnancy. As the deception expands, the prettiness becomes less comforting. It reveals how thoroughly a role can be staged before anyone asks what it costs the person performing it.

Alberdi’s reenactments do not pretend to be recovered reality. Their brightness and precision expose their artificiality, turning the fake pregnancy into a story told through another visible fabrication. That double construction is risky. The actor’s expressiveness and the production design can make the perpetrator’s perspective emotionally dominant, while the victim’s experience receives less time. Sight and Sound’s review identifies that imbalance as a genuine ethical problem rather than a flaw the film can solve with a final disclaimer.

Yet the artifice also prevents viewers from treating reconstruction as proof. A familiar true-crime dramatization often hides its inventions behind naturalistic acting and neutral color. *A Child of My Own* makes invention impossible to overlook. The audience is asked to feel the pull of the story and notice the machinery producing that feeling at the same time.

## Alberdi keeps moving the border between documentary and fiction

Alberdi’s documentaries have often approached vulnerable lives through intimacy rather than interrogation. *The Mole Agent* placed an older man inside a care home under the loose premise of an investigation, while *The Eternal Memory* observed a marriage living with illness and the erosion of memory. In each case, the structure created access but also became part of what the film was examining.

Here the hybrid method is more confrontational because the underlying act is a crime. The film reportedly spent years in production and uses performers alongside the real people and archival traces connected to the case. Its two halves do not lock neatly together: dramatization invites identification, then documentary material destabilizes what the viewer thought had been understood.

That instability is the point. A headline organizes responsibility quickly. Memory, testimony and performance do not. Alberdi does not have to claim that all versions are equally true to show that different forms make different facts visible. A surveillance image can establish movement; an interview can reveal how someone now narrates a decision; a staged scene can expose the fantasy through which that decision became possible. None can replace the others.

## Understanding pressure does not redistribute guilt

The film’s reporting context emphasizes miscarriages, family expectations and the belief that womanhood required motherhood. Those pressures deserve examination because they help explain why the deception could be sustained and socially rewarded for months. They do not transfer responsibility for the abduction to an abstract culture.

This is where the film’s moral grey areas need precise language. Social pressure can narrow a person’s imagined choices without eliminating agency. Compassion for suffering can coexist with recognition of the suffering inflicted on someone else. The victim does not need to become less important for the perpetrator to become more comprehensible.

A stronger true-crime culture would be able to hold those propositions together. Too often the genre alternates between monstrosity and exoneration because both are easy to serialize. Alberdi’s method asks whether cinema can sustain an account in which causation is expansive and responsibility remains specific.

## The film makes the viewer’s appetite visible

Netflix describes *A Child of My Own* as a documentary, but its attraction also depends on the promise of a story stranger than fiction. The fake pregnancy and hospital abduction can be marketed as irresistible twists before the audience encounters the women whose lives supplied them. Alberdi cannot stand outside that economy; the film participates in it by reconstructing the deception with stars, sets and carefully designed images.

What distinguishes the project is its willingness to show that participation. Behind-the-scenes material and shifts in form prevent the narrative from becoming a sealed spectacle. They remind viewers that access was negotiated, memories were selected and moral emphasis was created in the edit.

That self-awareness does not automatically correct every imbalance. The relative absence of the victim’s perspective remains consequential, and viewers may reasonably decide that the film’s empathy is distributed unfairly. But the disagreement is more useful than the passive certainty offered by a procedural recap. It asks not only what judgment the case deserves, but how images train us to deliver it.

*A Child of My Own* reaches a mass audience with no shortage of dramatic hooks. Its more lasting provocation is quieter: every true-crime story puts someone in the witness box, but it also builds the courtroom and chooses where the audience sits.
